question.en: What is WCAG, and how should a frontend engineer use it?

answer.en: WCAG is the W3C Web Content Accessibility Guidelines. It organizes requirements under four principles: content should be perceivable, operable, understandable, and robust. Success criteria have conformance levels, but a team should not treat a level label as a substitute for user-centered testing. I use the criteria to turn accessibility requirements into design, markup, CSS, and interaction checks—for example, keyboard operation, visible focus, text alternatives, labels, and programmatically exposed names and states. Automated checks are useful for repeatable rules, while manual keyboard and assistive-technology testing are still necessary.

question.en: An automated audit reports zero violations. Is the page conformant?

answer.en: No conclusion follows. Automated checks cover a repeatable subset of rules; keyboard operation, focus and reading order, alt-text quality, name and state correctness, and real assistive-technology behavior all require manual judgment. Use automation for regression coverage and pair it with manual keyboard and screen-reader passes.

question.en: When should you use ARIA, and when should you use native HTML instead?

answer.en: Native HTML is the default because the browser already supplies semantics, keyboard behavior, and accessibility-API mappings for standard controls. I add ARIA when the required role, state, property, or relationship cannot be expressed with native HTML, and then I implement the complete interaction as well. ARIA does not add behavior by itself. For example, putting a button role on a div does not automatically provide keyboard activation. I also avoid conflicting or redundant roles and verify the resulting accessible name, role, state, value, and focus behavior with inspection and manual testing.

question.en: aria-hidden="true" is added to a container that includes a button that is still focusable. What do keyboard screen-reader users experience?

answer.en: The button stays in the tab order, because aria-hidden does not remove focusability, but it is exposed with no name or role, so users tab into a silent, invisible stop. Hiding a focusable element this way is an explicit ARIA usage violation. Either keep the button outside the hidden subtree or hide it with the hidden attribute or display: none, which removes it from the tab order as well (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/Accessibility/ARIA/Attributes/aria-hidden).

question.en: Does adding aria-label="filters" to a plain non-interactive div give screen-reader users anything?

answer.en: Generally no. A generic div has no role that participates in naming, and aria-label is in practice only supported on interactive elements, widgets, landmarks, images, and iframes, so most screen readers ignore it there. Put the label on something that can be named: a real heading, a landmark, or the interactive control itself (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/Accessibility/ARIA/Attributes/aria-label).

question.en: What are name, role, state, and value, and why do they matter?

answer.en:
The accessible name identifies a component to the user; the role describes what it is; states and properties expose characteristics such as expanded, checked, or disabled; and the value communicates the current user-settable value where applicable. These must be programmatically determinable and changes must be exposed to user agents and assistive technology. Standard HTML controls usually provide this contract when used correctly. For custom widgets, I explicitly design the semantic mapping, keyboard interaction, focus model, and state updates together. An ARIA attribute without matching behavior can expose a misleading interface. ```html caption="The state and relationship must reflect the actual control behavior."
...
```

question.en: A button shows the visible text 'Submit' and carries aria-label="Send". What is announced, and why is that a problem?

answer.en: 'Send'. The name computation prefers aria-label over the element's content, so the visible text is replaced. Speech-input users who say 'click Submit' may get no match, because WCAG 2.5.3 Label in Name expects the visible label text to be contained in the accessible name. Make them identical, or start the accessible name with the visible text (https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Understanding/label-in-name.html).

question.en: You need to attach a longer hint ('We will only use this for order updates') to an input. aria-labelledby or aria-describedby?

answer.en: aria-describedby. It adds a description announced after the field, while the label stays the concise accessible name. aria-labelledby would replace the name with the whole sentence, so every navigation of the field reads a paragraph instead of its identity. The same describedby pattern is where error messages belong (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/Accessibility/ARIA/Attributes/aria-describedby).

question.en: How do you make a custom interactive element keyboard accessible?

answer.en:
First I ask whether a native button, link, input, or disclosure control already fits; that is safer. If custom markup is unavoidable, it needs an interactive role, a programmatically determinable name, keyboard activation equivalent to pointer activation, a sensible place in the tab order, and a visible focus indicator. A tabindex value of zero adds an element to the normal order; a value of negative one permits programmatic focus without adding it to sequential tabbing. I avoid positive tabindex values because they create a separate order that is hard to maintain and can confuse users.

```html caption="Prefer a native button and preserve a visible focus treatment."
<button class="control" type="button">Save</button>

<style>
.control:focus-visible { outline: 3px solid currentColor; outline-offset: 3px; }
</style>
```

question.en: A designer asks you to remove the focus outline because it looks bad. When is outline: none acceptable?

answer.en: Only when it is replaced immediately with an equally visible, contrasting focus treatment, for example a custom outline or shadow on :focus-visible. Every keyboard-focusable control needs a visible indicator for as long as focus is present, so removal without replacement is never acceptable.

question.en: Does adding tabindex="0" to a div make it accessible?

answer.en: No. It becomes focusable but still has no role and no name, so screen readers announce nothing meaningful at that stop, and activation still has to be hand-built. A custom control needs an interactive role, a programmatically determinable name, keyboard activation, a sensible place in the tab order, and a visible focus indicator, all together. If a native button, link, or input fits, that is the safer choice.

question.en: How should you provide alternative text for meaningful and decorative images?

answer.en: Alternative text should convey the image's relevant meaning in its context, not blindly describe every visible detail. A meaningful image gets concise `alt` text; if nearby text already communicates the same information, the alternative should not duplicate it. A purely decorative image should use an empty `alt` so assistive technology can skip it, or be supplied as CSS decoration when appropriate. An absent `alt` is not equivalent to an intentional empty alternative. If an image needs a longer explanation, provide that as surrounding text and associate it deliberately rather than putting an essay in `alt`. ```html caption="The first image conveys identity; the second is decorative." ```

question.en: What is the practical difference between alt="", a missing alt attribute, and role="presentation" on an img?

answer.en: alt="" is an intentional declaration that the image is decorative, so assistive technology skips it. A missing alt is unspecified: screen readers may announce the filename or the image's presence, forcing users to guess. role="presentation" or role="none" also strips the image's semantics, but the empty alt is the first-line, broadly supported way to say 'decorative'.

question.en: A logo image sits inside the home link, and the word 'Home' is visible next to it. What should the img's alt be?

answer.en: Empty. The link already gets its accessible name from the visible 'Home' text, and alt text inside a link contributes to the link's name, so 'Home' or 'ACME logo' would make the link announce twice or replace better text. If the logo were the link's only content, its alt should give the destination ('Home'), not describe the pixels ('Company logo').

question.en: When would an `aria-live` region be appropriate, and how would you avoid overwhelming users?

answer.en:
A live region is appropriate when content changes dynamically and the user needs the update without moving focus, such as a concise status or validation result. I prefer native elements and purpose-specific roles where they fit, keep the announced text short, and choose politeness based on urgency: routine updates should not interrupt, while urgent messages may need stronger announcement behavior. I do not put an entire frequently changing dashboard in an assertive region. I also test with the target browser and screen reader combination, because announcement timing and support are part of the real user experience. ```html caption="A concise, non-interruptive status is a reasonable live-region use."

Saved.

```

question.en: After a user action, a status div is created and filled with text in the same operation, but nothing is announced. Why might that happen?

answer.en: Live-region announcements are most reliable when the region already exists in the accessibility tree before its content changes. A region inserted and populated at the same time is not reliably picked up across browser and screen-reader combinations. Keep a persistent region, for example one with role="status", in the DOM and update its text, then verify with the exact browser and screen-reader pair you ship to (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/Accessibility/ARIA/Guides/Live_regions).

question.en: When is aria-live="assertive" actually justified?

answer.en: Rarely: only for urgent, time-sensitive messages where interrupting the user is the right call, for example a session about to expire or a destructive action about to run. Routine feedback such as 'Saved' or 'Results updated' should be polite, so it waits for the current utterance instead of trampling it.

question.en: What should an accessible focus indicator and hover-triggered disclosure do?

answer.en:
Every keyboard-focusable control needs a visible focus indicator, and it must remain visible while focus is present. I preserve the browser indicator or replace it with a sufficiently clear, contrasting style rather than removing it. If hover or focus reveals additional content, users need a way to dismiss it without moving focus, the pointer must be able to move into the content without it disappearing, and the content should persist until the trigger is left, it is dismissed, or it is no longer valid. The pattern must work with keyboard, touch, zoom, and assistive technology—not only a mouse.

```css caption="Keep focus visible; style can be customized without removing the indication."
:focus-visible { outline: 3px solid currentColor; outline-offset: 3px; }
```

question.en: A tooltip appears on hover of an info icon and disappears before the pointer can reach it. Which requirement is missed, and what are the others?

answer.en: Hoverable: the pointer must be able to move into the revealed content without it disappearing. The full set for content shown on hover or focus is dismissible (Esc or moving away dismisses it without advancing focus or the pointer), hoverable, and persistent (it stays until dismissed, the trigger is left, or it is no longer valid). All three must hold for keyboard, touch, zoom, and assistive technology, not only a mouse (https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/quickref/).

question.en: Why style :focus-visible instead of :focus for the custom focus indicator?

answer.en: :focus applies on every focus, including mouse clicks, so a custom ring shows in places where it adds noise and designers then demand its removal. :focus-visible matches when the browser determines an indicator is appropriate, typically keyboard interaction, keeping click interactions clean while keyboard users still always get a visible indicator.

question.en: How should a client-rendered route change be made understandable to keyboard and screen-reader users?

answer.en: A client-rendered route change should update the document title and provide a clear focus destination in the new view, commonly the page heading or a main-region target. Focus should not remain on a control that disappeared, and it should not be moved without a meaningful reason. The new content needs correct headings, landmarks, names, and states so assistive technology can understand it. I preserve normal link semantics and browser history, announce only what is useful, and test back/forward navigation, deep links, loading and error states, keyboard traversal, and screen-reader reading order. The implementation belongs in the routing/accessibility platform layer rather than every page.

question.en: You move focus to the new view's h1 after a client-side route change. Why tabindex="-1" on the heading instead of 0?

answer.en: -1 makes the heading programmatically focusable without adding it to the sequential tab order, which is exactly what a momentary focus destination needs. With 0, the heading becomes a permanent tab stop on every page, adding a keystroke for keyboard users just to support one focus move.

question.en: Why not just fire an aria-live announcement like 'Settings page loaded' on every navigation?

answer.en: Route changes already have a richer established signal: update the document title and move focus to the new heading or main region, which gives users the page identity and a reading position. A generic live message adds a second, vaguer channel that can double-announce or interrupt, and it says nothing about the content's structure. Announce only what is useful.
